blocks.text: But the Arabs who translated it as parrot took the Aleph in the word אנפה anapha to stand for Ajin, so that it would be derived from ענף anaph, which means branch; and hence the name was given to the parrot, because it hangs its nest from the branches of trees ^{(3)}. Cadamosto, in chapter 30 of his Navigations: These birds have a wonderful skill and ingenuity in nest-building. For they seek out a very tall tree which has slender and thin twigs, scarcely able to bear any weight at all. To the tip of these they tie a hanging twig, from which they suspend the nest, built with wonderful industry, round like a ball, leaving only an opening, very narrow, which serves as a door. They say the bird does this to outwit the cunning of serpents. Gesner reports the very same from Petrus Gillius, page 723. And the Arabs attribute the same industry to the bird thenavvut. Alcamus: التنوط طاير يدلي خيوطا من شجرة وينسج عشه كقارورة الدهن منوطا بتلك الخيوط [al-tanawwuṭ ṭāʾir yudlī khuyūṭan min shajara wa-yansuju ʿushshahu ka-qārūrat al-duhn manūṭan bi-tilka al-khuyūṭ] Thenavvut (as if you were to say the hanging bird) is a certain bird which hangs a thread from a tree and weaves its nest like a flask of oil, suspended from that thread. Alasmius: انما سمي بذلك لانه يدلي خيطا من شجرة [innamā summiya bi-dhālika li-annahu yudlī khayṭan min shajara] [III, 105] يفرخ فيها [yufarrikhu fīhā] It is so called, namely, because it hangs a thread from the tree in which it nests; for نوط [nawṭ] means to hang. On the same bird Damir: من شانه انه اذا اقبل الليل اخذ بغصن شجرة ويضم عليه رجليه وينكس راسه ثم لا يزال يصبح حتي يطلع النور [min shaʾnihi annahu idhā aqbala al-layl akhadha bi-ghuṣn shajara wa-yaḍummu ʿalayhi rijlayhi wa-yunakkisu raʾsahu thumma lā yazālu yuṣbiḥu ḥattā yaṭluʿa al-nūr] It is its nature that, when night comes on, it takes hold of a branch of a tree, clasping its feet to it, with its head bent downward, and does not stop singing until day dawns ^{(4)}. Amusing [col. 342] is what some add: وانما يفعل ذلك خوفا من السما تقع عليه [wa-innamā yafʿalu dhālika khawfan min al-samā taqaʿu ʿalayhi] that it does this lest the sky fall upon it. Like the Germans who, when asked by Alexander what they feared, answered that they feared only this, that the sky might fall. But, to return to the parrot: like the peacock, discussed above ^{e)}, I could hardly believe that the parrot was known to the Jews in the age of Moses. For it is an Indian bird. Writers testify to this with great agreement. Thus Ctesias writes in the Indica, as quoted by Photius, περὶ τοῦ ὀρνέου τοῦ βιττάκου, ὅτι γλῶσσαν ἀνθρωπίνην ἔχει, καὶ φωνὴν [peri tou orneou tou bittakou, hoti glōssan anthrōpinēn echei, kai phōnēn], concerning the bird bittacus, [III, 106] (as they then called it) that it has a human tongue and voice. Arrian also in the Indica: Σιττακοὺς δὲ Νέαρχος μὲν ὡς δή τι θαῦμα ἀπηγέεται, ὅτι γίγνονται ἐν τῇ Ἰνδῶν γῇ, καὶ ὁποῖος ὄρνις ἐστὶν ὁ σιττακὸς, καὶ ὅπως φωνὴν ἵει ἀνθρωπίνην [Sittakous de Nearchos men hōs dē ti thauma apēgeetai, hoti gignontai en tē Indōn gē, kai hopoios ornis estin ho sittakos, kai hopōs phōnēn hiei anthrōpinēn]. Nearchus (who campaigned with Alexander) relates as a kind of marvel that sittaci are born in India, and what sort of bird the sittacus is, and how it utters a human voice. From this you may gather that parrots were not yet known in Greece at that time. Aristotle, History, book 8, chapter 12: Καὶ τὸ Ἰνδικὸν ὄρνεον ἡ ψιττακὴ, τὸ λεγόμενον ἀνθρωπόγλωττον [Kai to Indikon orneon hē psittakē, to legomenon anthrōpoglōtton]; And the Indian bird, the parrot, which is said to have a human tongue. Pliny, book 10, chapter 42: India, however, sends this bird; it calls it psittace. Aelian, History, book 16, chapter 2: Ἐν Ἰνδοῖς μανθάνω σιττακοὺς ὄρνις γίνεσθαι [En Indois manthanō sittakous ornis ginesthai]. I hear that sittacus birds are bred among the Indians. See also book 13, chapter 18, and book 16, chapter 15. Pausanias in the Corinthiaca: Παρὰ δὲ Ἰνδῶν μόνων ἄλλα τε κομίζεται, καὶ ὄρνιθες οἱ ψιττακοί [Para de Indōn monōn alla te komizetai, kai ornithes hoi psittakoi]. From the Indians alone are brought both other things and parrots. Apuleius, Florida, book 2: The parrot is a bird of India. Solinus, chapter 52: India alone sends the parrot bird. Philostorgius, book 3, where he speaks of the lands lying toward the farthest East and South: Καὶ μὲν δὴ καὶ τὴν σιττακὴν ἐκεῖθεν ἴσμεν νομιζομένην [Kai men dē kai tēn sittakēn ekeithen ismen nomizomenēn]; And indeed we know that the parrot too is brought from there. Hence Ovid, Amores, book 2, Elegy 6:
The parrot, a bird sent to me from the Eastern Indians.
The parrot, a gift given from the farthest edge of the world.
That parrot, green ruler of the Eastern region.
And the old Poet in the Riddle On the Parrot:
The Indian land bore me on its purple shore, where the bright day returns as the orb is kindled.
